**Summary of Work Completed**

**What I did:**  
Performed targeted web searches for medical sources covering week 6 (days 36‑42) postpartum, focusing on four domains: infant sleep maturation, maternal return‑to‑work considerations, breastfeeding continuation, and postpartum depression awareness. For each domain, I collected peer‑reviewed articles, clinical guidelines, and reputable health‑organization resources. I attempted to extract full‑text content from the most relevant URLs using the `web_extract` tool, but encountered a backend limitation (the free Brave Search tier only supports search, not content extraction).

**What I found / Accomplished:**  
Below is a curated list of high‑quality sources for each topic, with titles, URLs, and brief descriptions derived from search results.

---

### 1. Infant Sleep Maturation (Week 6)
| Source | URL | Description |
|--------|-----|-------------|
| Infant Sleep Difficulties at the 6th Week and the 12th Month Postpartum: What Is their Relationship with Maternal Mental Health and Other Perinatal Factors? | https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116102/ | Examines how infant sleep difficulties at 6 weeks relate to maternal mental health (EPDS scores), fatigue, reflux, and other perinatal factors. |
| Infant sleep development from 3 to 6 months postpartum: links with maternal sleep and paternal involvement | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25704738/ | Shows maternal sleep predicts infant sleep; increased paternal caregiving improves both maternal and infant sleep in the first 6 months. |
| Baby Care: 6 Week Old Baby | https://www.huggies.com/en-us/resources/newborns-and-infants/baby-care/6-week-old-baby | Notes longer overnight sleep periods may emerge at 6 weeks, but parental fatigue often persists. |
| Understanding and identifying the 6‑week sleep regression and growth spurt | https://www.aumio.com/en/article/identifying-6-week-sleep-regression-growth-spurt | Explains the 6‑week regression as a neurodevelopmental shift where sleep patterns mature toward adult‑like cycles. |

### 2. Maternal Return‑to‑Work Considerations (Week 6)
| Source | URL | Description |
|--------|-----|-------------|
| Going back to work after baby: Timelines and tips | https://www.babycenter.com/baby/postpartum-health/when-can-i-go-back-to-work-after-delivery_1156149 | Highlights ACOG’s recommendation for ongoing postpartum care up to 12 weeks; 6 weeks is a traditional but not universal return‑to‑work point. |
| When to Return to Work After Giving Birth | https://www.babymed.com/daily-living/when-work-after-giving-birth | States that in most cases women are cleared to return to work at 6 weeks postpartum, depending on recovery and job type. |
| Work Reentry After Childbirth: Predictors of Self‑Rated Health in Month One Among a Sample of University Faculty and Staff | https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7078554/ | Investigates how early return‑to‑work affects self‑rated health, emphasizing physical and psychological sequelae of childbirth. |
| Optimizing Postpartum Care | https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care | ACOG committee opinion advising postpartum contact within the first 3 weeks and ongoing care; notes that traditional 6‑week visits may miss opportunities for breastfeeding support and depression screening. |

### 3. Breastfeeding Continuation (Week 6)
| Source | URL | Description |
|--------|-----|-------------|
| Breastfeeding continuation at 6 weeks postpartum remediates the negative effects of prenatal intimate partner violence on infant temperament | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30880656/ | Finds that breastfeeding at 6 weeks acts as a protective factor, mitigating the impact of prenatal IPV on infant temperament outcomes at 4 months. |
| Postpartum Care of the New Mother - StatPearls | https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK565875/ | Covers lactational amenorrhea method criteria and general postpartum lactation support. |
| Essential Guide: Breastfeeding at 3‑6 Weeks Postpartum | https://physicianguidetobreastfeeding.org/breastfeeding-basics/next-steps-3-6-weeks/ | Discusses common challenges (e.g., colic, growth spurts) and strategies to maintain milk production during weeks 3‑6. |
| Optimizing Postpartum Care (ACOG) | https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care | Notes that among women with early, undesired weaning, 20% discontinue breastfeeding by 6 weeks postpartum, underscoring the importance of timely lactation support. |

### 4. Postpartum Depression Awareness (Week 6)
| Source | URL | Description |
|--------|-----|-------------|
| Routine screening for postpartum depression | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11219558/ | Demonstrates that implementing routine EPDS screening at 6 weeks postpartum increased diagnosed PPD rates in the community. |
| Can We Screen for Postpartum Depression Earlier? – MGH Center for Women's Mental Health | https://womensmentalhealth.org/posts/postpartum-depression-screening/ | Shows EPDS at 2‑3 days postpartum has good predictive value for depressive symptoms emerging between 4‑6 weeks. |
| Screening for depression in the postpartum period: a comparison of three instruments | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18345995/ | Finds phone‑administered EPDS at 6‑8 weeks postpartum is an efficient, accurate way to identify high‑risk women within the first 6 months. |
| The Identification of Postpartum Depression – PMC – NIH | https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2736559/ | Recommends optimal PPD screening timing at 4‑6 weeks post‑delivery; EPDS ≥13 is a common cut‑off for detection. |
